description.narrative:
Objectives
The project seeks to fullfil four key objectives:
1. Support national longitudinal mixed-methods studies of government-run cash-based programmes to understand design and implementation and examine their impacts, including on:
a) Gender equality and women's empowerment b) Long-term impacts including adolescent transitions to adulthood c) Urban areas d) People with disability e) Resilience to shocks through cash transfers and shock-responsive cash-based programming.
2. Generate evidence on public finance for sustainable social protection including political economy analysis of the decisions to invest in social protection.
3. Undertake country-level and cross-country analysis to respond to evidence gaps on social transfer programmes and social protection systems in the region.
4. Facilitate mechanisms for learning and exchange among regional policymakers, implementers, researchers and civil society through workshops, web resources, public data availability and open-access publications.

UNICEF Innocenti - Global Office of Research and Foresight, has applied for SEK 19,000,000 to implement the research programme ‘the Transfer Projects’ fourth phase, 2025-2027. Sida's management of the operation has been delegated to the Unit for Eastern Africa and the Horn of Africa from five embassies, these are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
The programme aims to enable policy makers to base policy decisions on policy and further development of the country's social protection system on evidence from solid research and experience.
The research programme has four objectives, these are to: 1. Support national longitudinal mixed-methods studies of government-run cash-based programmes to understand design and implementation and examine their impacts, including on: a) Gender equality and women's empowerment b) Long-term impacts including adolescent transitions to adulthood c) Urban areas d) People with disability e) Resilience to shocks through cash transfers and shock-responsive cash-based programming. 2. Generate evidence on public finance for sustainable social protection . 3. Undertake country-level and cross-country analysis. 4. Facilitate mechanisms for learning and exchange among regional policymakers, implementers, researchers and civil society.
Expected outputs include: baseline data, reports, peer-reviewed articles published in reputable journals, policy and research information, capacity building for African researchers, and presentations in workshops or at international conferences.
It is Sida's assessment that the project proposal is relevant and justified.

Unicefs forskningsinstitut, Innocenti, har ansökt om 19 000 000 SEK för att genomföra forskningsprogrammet "the Transfer Projects” fjärde fas, 2025-2027. Sidas hantering av insatsen har delegerats till Enheten för Östafrika och Afrikas Horn från fem ambassader, dessa är Etiopien, Kenya, Mocambique, Zambia och Zimbabwe.
Programmets syfte är att ge beslutsfattare möjligheten att basera politiska beslut om policy och vidareutveckling av landets system för social trygghet på fakta från gedigen forskning och erfarenheter.
Forskningsprogrammet har fyra huvudmål, dessa är att: 1. Stödja nationella longitudinella studier med blandade metoder av statligt drivna kontantbaserade program för att förstå utformning och genomförande och undersöka deras effekter, bland annat på: a) jämställdhet och kvinnors egenmakt b) långsiktiga effekter av social trygghet, inklusive ungdomars övergång till vuxenlivet c) utveckling av social trygghet i urbana områden d) och för människor som lever med funktionshinder samt d) motståndskraft mot chocker genom kontantöverföringar och social trygghet anpassad att verka effektivt när samhällen drabbas av chocker. 2. Ta fram bevis på offentlig finansiering för hållbara sociala trygghets system. 3. Genomföra analyser på landnivå. 4. Underlätta mekanismer för lärande och utbyte
Förväntade resultat inkluderar: grunddata, rapporter, expertgranskade artiklar publicerade i välrenomerade tidsskrifter, policy och forskningsinformation, kapacitetsuppbyggnad för afrikanska forskare samt presentationer i workshops eller vid internationella konferenser.
Sida bedömer att insatsen är relevant och motiverad.

sector.narrative: Social protection and welfare services policy, planning and administration

description.narrative:
This is the first year that the program is being implemented, which means that this year's activities have been focused on dialogue, coordination and planning of relevant research interventions. Also, procurement of actors who collect data, etc. Information from the Plan and Budget 2026 show that activities are ongoing in all five countries. In addition briefs and articles based on research from the previous phase is still published and discussed.
In relation to the first objective work is ongoing in Ethiopia, Kenya and Mozambique:
In Ethiopia UNICEF Innocenti is collaborating with the Ministry of Women and Social Affairs and UNICEF Ethiopia on a longitudinal mixed-methods study of the child grant programme. Research will assess the outcomes of the child grant programme, including nutrition-related outcomes among young children and pregnant women, child well-being, intra-household decision-making on child grant use, financial resource management, womens empowerment, uptake of health care services, caregiver knowledge about feeding practices and household resilience. Baseline data collection is scheduled for December 2025/January 2026. Research briefs, that can be used for visibility and sharing of results will be produced after each data collection round.
UNICEF Innocenti is collaborating with the Kenyan Government and UNICEF Kenya on research that will examine the long-term effects of the Cash Transfer for Orphan and Vulnerable Children (CT-OVC). The CT-OVC programme is a long-standing social protection programme that was initiated with Sida's support, in 2004. today it reaches 440,000 poor households across the country. Here the research will focus on long-term results in a study relying on qualitative methods. It will include an evidence summary of the impact of the programme on households and children, based on previously published reports and studies. Next, qualitative data collection will be conducted to assess (i) the well-being trajectories and major life events of original beneficiary children, (ii) long-term impacts on their health and education as adults, (iii) intergenerational impacts on the health and education of children of the original beneficiaries, and (iv) the operational factors that moderated the long-term and intergenerational impacts. The final arrangements for the evidence summary and data collection is ongoing. In Kenya the planning of research activities were delayed in as both Kenya's social department and UNICEF Kenya had reduced budgets and number of staff after USAID was closed down, which delayed the opportunity for dialogue and decisions on research. During the autumn, dialogue and planning have continued according to plan.
In Mozambique UNICEF Innocenti is collaborating with the government and UNICEF Mozambique on a study of the Child Grant programme. The Child Grant programme commenced as a pilot in 2018 and targets children 0-2 years old. An impact evaluation was conducted in collaboration with UNICEF Innocenti researchers between 2019 and 2021. The evaluation found positive impacts of the cash transfers on household economic standing and food security, ability to cope with shocks, well-being of caregivers, child-level material well-being and time use etc, while the case management led to a reduction in intimate partner violence and violent discipline against children. Building upon the previous evaluation, UNICEF Innocenti will carry out research to assess the long-term effects of participation in the Child Grant Pilot as measured by well-being trajectories, and long-term outcomes, while comparing the differences in effects between cash-only households and cash and care, as well as beneficiaries that were identified as low-risk versus high-risk cases. A scoping mission is ongoing.
In relation to the second objective work is ongoing in Ethiopia, Kenya, Zambia and Zimbabwe:
In Ethiopia UNICEF Innocenti is collaborating with MoWSA, UNICEF Ethiopia and other partners to co-create country appropriate scenarios for developing the cost of inaction and an investment case for social protection in the country. Discussions on the choice of policy options is ongoing.
In Kenya UNICEF Innocenti is collaborate with UNICEF Kenya on a study that will model the extent to which economic growth has translated into poverty reduction and improved living standards for households, over the past two decades. The study will utilize existing surveys, including the Kenya Integrated Household Budget Survey (KIHBS), the Kenya Continuous Household Survey (KCHS) and the Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (DHS). A scoping review is ongoing.
In Zambia: UNICEF Innocenti will collaborate with UNICEF Zambia, the government and other partners to co-create country appropriate scenarios for developing the cost of inaction and an investment case for social protection in the country. Initial discussions with UNU-WIDER are underway to explore the possibility of collaboration given their ongoing related work with UNICEF Zambia. A final scope of work currently being developed with UNICEF Zambia is ongoing.
In Zimbabwe UNICEF Innocenti will collaborate with the government, UNICEF Zimbabwe and Development Pathways on a study on the fiscal implications for a new social protection portfolio in Zimbabwe, along with the expected effects on poverty and inequality. Consultations are ongoing to define the final scope of the study by the end of December 2025.
In relation to the third objective researchers are writing and revising at least eleven papers, including a cross-country research paper examining the impacts of cash plus programmes on womens labour market participation, a study that determines the willingness to pay for community health insurance in Ethiopia, another on the qualitative impacts of the universal child benefit pilot in Kenya, a and another examining the longer-term impacts of the adolescent cash plus programme on economic activities and time use in Tanzania.
In the fourth objective training of local researchers is ongoing and a first workshop implemented jointly with the African Evaluation Association and American Institutes of Research is finalised.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
